summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Bashkortostan has no division-specific provisions or reporting in the available sources. A visitor to the republic stands under the national framework as applied countrywide, and the UK Home Office note is explicit that no division-specific information about Bashkortostan appears in it.

Under that national framework, same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. The "gay propaganda" law makes public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition punishable by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, and a repeated offence can bring up to four years' imprisonment. Displaying rainbow symbols falls within the prohibition. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023; between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws.

The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia regardless of personal characteristics. It warns that foreigners found guilty under the "propaganda" law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is itself a crime.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) reports that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its symbols since the November 2023 designation, with penalties of up to 12 years in prison. HRW also identified 81 people in 98 cases found guilty since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The 2013 "gay propaganda" law had already made any positive or neutral depiction of non-heterosexual relations an administrative offence.
tangentialFactors:
Two enforcement tracks run in parallel and a visitor can fall into either. The administrative track under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses produced 98 cases against 81 people between January and June 2025 for displaying banned symbols, most of them on social media, while the criminal extremism track has produced 101 convictions carrying penalties of up to 12 years. The 2013 propaganda statute already treated positive or neutral depictions of non-heterosexual relations as an administrative offence, so the post-2023 regime widened an existing enforcement habit rather than creating a new one.

Volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza's reporting of 19 June 2025 puts propaganda-law cases at eighteen times the level of a decade earlier and records more than 60 million rubles collected in fines over two years, indicating routine, revenue-generating enforcement rather than isolated prosecutions.

The designation moved fast against public venues. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling in November 2023, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, holding about 100 patrons at one venue against walls for search and photography, with at least two further venues raided the same night. Queer Russians described by The Moscow Times on 23 June 2025 characterise their standing after the designation as that of a second-class citizen.

Custodial risk is not theoretical. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a man held on extremism charges connected to an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Transgender people also face coercive treatment outside the criminal process: BBC Russian documented a transgender woman held for nine months from summer 2021 in a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, forced to take testosterone and perform manual labour.

The UK asylum standard treats LGBT+ people across the whole country, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, which means countrywide exposure is recognised even where reporting concentrates on other cities.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bashkortostan live under the same national statutes as visitors, with the added exposure of being subject to prosecution rather than deportation. Same-sex sexual activity carries no penalty, but marriage to a same-sex partner and legal gender transition are unavailable, and gender-affirming healthcare has been effectively unavailable since 2023.

Ordinary online conduct carries administrative liability. Article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses has been applied to 81 people in 98 cases since January 2024 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, overwhelmingly in social media posts, and the 2013 propaganda law already made positive or neutral depictions of non-heterosexual relations an administrative offence before the expansion.

Repeat or aggravated expression escalates to criminal punishment. Individuals fined up to 400,000 rubles or detained for up to 15 days for a first propaganda offence face up to four years' imprisonment on repetition, and participation in or display of symbols of the designated extremist movement carries up to 12 years. At least 139 individuals were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

Residents have no domestic legal route to recognition of a trans identity or a same-sex partnership, and the extremist designation exposes community organising and mutual-aid activity to the same charges. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to people leaving the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement, court decisions or local policy specific to Bashkortostan. Whether the republic's interior ministry or courts have issued extremism or article 20.3 decisions since November 2023 is unresolved and not sourced here.

The UK Home Office note states that no division-specific information about Bashkortostan appears in it, so the republic-level assessment rests entirely on the national framework. Whether any Bashkortostan authority applies the national statutes more or less strictly than the national average is not sourced.

The figure of at least 139 individuals impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 is given without a breakdown by charge type, region or outcome in the available material.

The reference to Chechnya in the UK Home Office note concerns a different republic and does not establish conditions in Bashkortostan; it is cited only for the countrywide particular-social-group standard.

Whether the conversion-therapy detention documented near Novosibirsk reflects a pattern in Bashkortostan is unresolved; the single reported case is from a different part of the country.
